1.1: As I am about to show a deeply philosophical point—that reverent reasoning is the true master over the emotions—I encourage you to pay close attention to this wisdom.
1.2: Reason is essential for everyone as a foundation for knowledge, and it includes the praise of self-control, which is the highest virtue.
1.3: If reasoning is shown to have control over emotions that oppose self-restraint, like gluttony and lust,
1.4: then it clearly also rules over feelings that go against justice, such as malice, and those that hinder courage, like anger, pain, and fear.
1.5: Some might ask, “If reasoning rules the emotions, why doesn’t it also control forgetfulness and ignorance?” This is a mistaken argument.
1.6: Reasoning does not rule over its own abilities, but over emotions that oppose justice, courage, temperance, and self-control; and it does so by resisting them, not by destroying them.
1.7: I could show you in many ways that reverent reasoning is the only master of the emotions;
1.8: but I will prove it most strongly by the courage of Eli’ezer, his seven relatives, and their mother, who gave their lives for virtue.
1.9: All of them, by treating pain with contempt even to death, showed through their endurance that reasoning rules over the emotions.
1.10: Because of their virtues, I should praise these people who died with their mother at this time for the sake of nobility and goodness; and for their honor, I count them happy.
1.11: They earned admiration not only from everyone, but even from their persecutors, for their courage and endurance. By their perseverance, they helped bring down the tyranny against their nation, overcoming the tyrant and purifying their country.
1.12: Now, let us begin our discussion, as is our custom, by stating the principle, and then move on to the story of these people, giving esteem to the all-wise Elohim.
1.13: So the question is whether reasoning is truly master over the emotions.
1.14: Let’s consider what reasoning is, what emotion is, how many types of emotions there are, and whether reasoning rules over all of them.
1.15: Reasoning is the mind guided by a life of righteousness, always putting wisdom first.
1.16: Wisdom is the knowledge of matters both divine and human, and their causes.
1.17: This is taught in the instruction of the Torah, through which we learn about divine matters with reverence and human matters for our benefit.
1.18: The forms of wisdom are self-control, justice, courage, and temperance.
1.19: The greatest of these is self-control, by which reasoning truly rules over the emotions.
1.20: Of all emotions, pleasure and pain are the two main ones, and they naturally relate to the being.
1.21: There are many related feelings that surround pleasure and pain.
1.22: Lust comes before pleasure, and joy follows after pleasure.
1.23: Fear comes before pain, and sorrow follows after pain.
1.24: Anger is a feeling that can be connected to both pleasure and pain, if you pay attention when it arises.
1.25: Within pleasure there is a malicious tendency, which is the most complicated of all emotions.
1.26: In the being, this shows up as arrogance, greed, desire for honor, rivalry, unfaithfulness, and envy.
1.27: In the body, it appears as greediness, uncontrolled eating, and selfish gluttony.
1.28: Just as pleasure and pain grow from both body and being, so there are many offshoots of these emotions.
1.29: Reasoning, like a wise gardener, cleanses and trims each of these, tying up, watering, and transplanting, improving the qualities of our morals and feelings in every way.
1.30: Reasoning leads the virtues, but it is the only ruler of the emotions. So, first notice—by looking at the things that challenge self-control—that reasoning truly rules over the emotions.
1.31: Self-control means having command over our desires.
1.32: Some desires belong to the being, others to the body. Reasoning appears to rule over both.
1.33: Otherwise, why is it that when we are tempted by forbidden foods, we refuse the pleasure they would give? Isn’t it because reasoning can control our appetites? I believe so.
1.34: That’s why, when we crave seafood, birds, four-footed animals, and all kinds of food forbidden to us by the Torah, we hold ourselves back through the power of reasoning.
1.35: The desires of our appetites are resisted by a self-controlled mind, turned back, and all the impulses of the body are restrained by reasoning.

10.1: This one also faced a praiseworthy death. The third brother was brought forward and urged by many to taste the food and save his life.
10.2: But he cried out, saying, “Don’t you realize that the father of those who have died is my father too, and that we share the same mother, and I was raised just like them?
10.3: I will not deny the noble bond of my family.
10.4: So, whatever instrument of punishment you have, use it on my body, because you cannot touch my being, even if you want to.”
10.5: But they, furious at his bold words, dislocated his hands and feet with torture devices, and pulled them from their sockets, tearing him apart.
10.6: They dragged his fingers, arms, legs, and ankles around.
10.7: When they couldn’t strangle him by any means, they tore off his skin along with the tips of his fingers, and then dragged him to the wheel,
10.8: where his spine was pulled apart, and he saw his own flesh torn to pieces, with streams of blood flowing from his insides.
10.9: As he was about to die, he said,
10.10: “We, O cursed tyrant, endure this for the sake of Elohim’s teaching and virtue.
10.11: But you, because of your wickedness and bloodshed, will suffer endless torment.”
10.12: After he died, worthy of his family, they dragged forward the fourth brother, saying,
10.13: “Don’t share in the madness of your brothers, but respect the meleḵ and save yourself.”
10.14: But he replied, “You don’t have a fire hot enough to make me act like a coward.
10.15: By the happy death of my brothers, the everlasting punishment of the tyrant, and the esteemed life of the righteous, I will not deny the noble brotherhood.
10.16: Come up with new tortures, tyrant, so you may learn, even through them, that I am the brother of those who suffered before me.”
10.17: When he said this, the bloodthirsty, murderous, and profane Antioḵos ordered his tongue to be cut out.
10.18: But he said, “Even if you take away my ability to speak, Elohim still hears those who are silent.
10.19: Look, my tongue is outstretched—cut it off; even then, you won’t silence our reasoning.
10.20: We gladly give up our limbs for the sake of Elohim.
10.21: But Elohim will quickly judge you, since you cut off the tongue, the instrument of divine melody.”

11.1: When he had died, disfigured by his torture, the fifth brother stepped forward and said,
11.2: "I don’t plan, O tyrant, to escape the suffering that comes for the sake of uprightness.
11.3: Instead, I have come willingly, so that by my death you will owe shamayim vengeance and punishment for even more crimes.
11.4: You hater of uprightness and of people, what have we done that you take such pleasure in our blood?
11.5: Is it evil to you that we worship the Founder of all things and live according to His surpassing Torah?
11.6: But this deserves esteem, not torture,
11.7: if you were able to feel the higher things of humanity and had the hope of deliverance from Elohim.
11.8: But see now, since you are alienated from Elohim, you make war against those who are reverent toward Elohim."
11.9: As he said this, the guards tied him up and brought him to the torture rack,
11.10: where, binding his knees and fastening them with iron shackles, they bent his body over the wedge of the wheel; then his body was torn apart, like a scorpion.
11.11: With his breath trapped and his body strangled, he said,
11.12: "You do us a great favor, O tyrant, by allowing us to show our loyalty to the Torah through even greater suffering."
11.13: When he too had died, the sixth brother, still a youth, was brought out. When the tyrant asked if he would eat and be set free, he replied,
11.14: "I may be younger than my brothers, but in understanding I am just as old.
11.15: I was born and raised for the same purpose. We are ready to die for the same cause.
11.16: So if you think it is right to torture us for not eating what is unclean, then go ahead and torture!"
11.17: As he said this, they brought him to the wheel.
11.18: Stretched out on it, with his limbs pulled and dislocated, he was slowly roasted from below.
11.19: After heating sharp spits, they stabbed them into his back; and after piercing his sides, they burned away his insides.
11.20: While being tortured, he said, "O good and qodesh contest, in which for the sake of reverence, we brothers have been called to this arena of pain and have not been defeated.
11.21: For reverent understanding, O tyrant, cannot be conquered.
11.22: Armed with uprightness, I too will depart with my brothers.
11.23: I also carry with me a great Avenger, O creator of tortures and enemy of the truly reverent.
11.24: We six young men have destroyed your tyranny.
11.25: Isn’t your failure to overcome our reasoning, and to force us to eat the unclean, your defeat?
11.26: Your fire feels cold to us. Your racks are painless, and your violence is powerless.
11.27: For our defenders are not the guards of a tyrant, but those of the divine Torah. Because of this, we keep our reasoning unconquered."

12.1: When he too had endured happy martyrdom and died in the cauldron where he had been thrown, the seventh, the youngest of them all, stepped forward.
12.2: The tyrant, feeling pity for him—though he had been harshly rebuked by his own family—
12.3: saw him already bound in chains, brought him closer, and tried to persuade him, saying,
12.4: "You see the outcome of your family's madness, for they died in agony because they disobeyed. If you also disobey, you will be miserably tortured and die before your time.
12.5: But if you obey, you will become my friend and have authority over the affairs of the reign."
12.6: After encouraging him in this way, he sent for the boy’s mother, hoping that by showing her compassion for the loss of so many sons, he might persuade her, through the hope of saving the last one, to make him obey.
12.7: After his mother encouraged him in the Iḇri language, he said,
12.8: "Let me go so I can speak to the meleḵ and all his friends."
12.9: They were overjoyed at the young man’s promise and quickly released him.
12.10: He ran up to the pans and said,
12.11: "Wicked tyrant and most blasphemous man, weren’t you ashamed, after receiving prosperity and a reign from Elohim, to kill His servants and torture those who do righteousness?
12.12: Because of this, 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄’s vengeance is waiting for you—eternal fire and torment will cling to you forever.
12.13: Weren’t you ashamed, though you are just a man and yet so savage, to cut out the tongues of those like yourself and torture them after abusing them this way?
12.14: But they, dying bravely, fulfilled their duty to Elohim.
12.15: But you will groan as you deserve, for killing the defenders of righteousness without cause.
12.16: So," he continued, "I too, about to die,
12.18: I call on the Elohim of my fathers to show mercy to my people.
12.19: But as for you, whether alive or dead, He will punish you."
12.20: After praying this, he threw himself into the pans and died.

13.1: If the seven brothers despised suffering even to death, it is clear to everyone that righteous reasoning truly rules over the emotions.
13.2: For if they had eaten what was not qodesh, giving in to their emotions, we would say they had been defeated by them.
13.3: But that is not the case. Instead, by the reasoning that is praised by 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄, they overcame their emotions.
13.4: We cannot ignore the power of thoughtful reflection, for it won victory over both emotions and suffering.
13.5: So how can we deny that these men mastered their emotions through right reasoning, since they did not shrink back from the pain of fire?
13.6: Just as towers built in front of harbors break the threatening waves and make the way safe for ships entering port,
13.7: so the sevenfold tower of right reasoning in these young men, protecting the harbor of reverence, overcame the storm of emotions.
13.8: Having formed a qodesh choir of reverence, they encouraged each other, saying,
13.9: “Brothers, let us die together for the Torah. Let us imitate the three young men in Ashshur who faced the furnace without fear.
13.10: Let us not be afraid to show our reverence.”
13.11: One said, “Be strong, brother!” and another, “Endure bravely!”
13.12: Another said, “Remember where you come from; our father Yitsḥaq was willing to be offered up for the sake of reverence.”
13.13: All of them, looking at each other calmly and confidently, said, “Let us give our lives with all our heart to Elohim who gave them, and use our bodies to keep the Torah.
13.14: Let us not fear the one who thinks he can kill us;
13.15: for there is a great test of the being and the danger of everlasting torment waiting for those who break the command of Elohim.
13.16: So let us arm ourselves with self-control, which is true reasoning from above.
13.17: If we suffer like this, Aḇraham, Yitsḥaq, and Ya’aqoḇ will welcome us, and all the fathers will praise us.
13.18: As each brother was taken away, the rest cried out, “Do not shame us, brother, or betray those who died before you!”
13.19: You know well the bond of brotherhood, which the all-wise and Divine Providence has given from fathers to children, and formed in the mother’s womb.
13.20: These brothers spent the same time in their mother’s womb, were formed together, nourished by the same blood, and brought to life by the same breath.
13.21: They were born at the same intervals, nursed from the same source, and their brotherly beings grew up together in love.
13.22: Their bond grew even stronger through being raised together, daily companionship, shared education, and training in the Torah of Elohim.
13.23: Because of this deep brotherly love, the seven brothers had an even greater unity with each other.
13.24: Being taught in the same Torah, practicing the same virtues, and living a just life together, they strengthened this harmony among themselves.
13.25: Their shared passion for what is right and honorable deepened their goodwill and unity.
13.26: And as this worked together with reverence, their brotherly love became even more precious to them.
13.27: Yet, even though nature, companionship, and virtuous living increased their brotherly love, those who remained endured seeing their brothers, who suffered for their reverence, tortured even to death.

14.1: Even more than this, they encouraged each other in this suffering, so that they not only endured pain themselves, but even overcame their natural feelings of brotherly love.
14.2: Reason is more royal than a meleḵ, and freer than those who are free!
14.3: What a qodesh and harmonious unity among the seven brothers when it came to reverence for 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄!
14.4: None of the seven young men became cowardly or shrank back from death.
14.5: Instead, all of them, as if running toward immortality, hurried to face death through torture.
14.6: Just as hands and feet move in harmony with the being’s direction, so these qodesh young men agreed to die for the sake of reverence, as if inspired by the immortal being of reverence.
14.7: O qodesh seven, united in family! For just as there are seven days of creation, so with reverence,
14.8: the young men, gathered around the number seven, overcame the fear of suffering.
14.9: We now shudder just hearing about the suffering of these young men; but they not only saw and heard the threats carried out right in front of them, they endured it themselves and persevered—even through the pain of fire.
14.10: What could be more painful? The power of fire, being sharp and swift, quickly destroyed their bodies.
14.11: Don’t be surprised that reason ruled over these men in their suffering, when even a woman’s mind was able to despise even greater pain.
14.12: For the mother of these seven young men endured the torture of each of her children.
14.13: Think about how deep a parent’s love is, drawing everyone to share in affection,
14.14: since even animals without reason have a similar sympathy and love for their young as humans do.
14.15: Tame birds that live on our rooftops protect their chicks.
14.16: Others build nests and hatch their young on mountaintops, in deep valleys, or in the holes and tops of trees, and keep intruders away.
14.17: If they can’t do this, they fly around their young in distress, calling out in their own way, and save their offspring however they can.
14.18: But why should we focus on the sympathy for children shown by animals without reason?
14.19: Even bees, during honey-making season, attack anyone who comes near, and sting—like with a sword—those who approach their hive, driving them away even to death.
14.20: But even this natural sympathy for her children did not turn aside the mother of the young men, who had a spirit like that of Aḇraham.

15.1: O reasoning of the sons, ruling over the emotions, and reverence for 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 more precious to a mother than her children!
15.2: When the mother was faced with two choices—faithfulness to 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 and the temporary safety of her seven sons, offered on the condition of obeying a tyrant—
15.3: she chose the reverence for 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄, which according to Elohim leads to everlasting life.
15.4: How can I properly describe the natural love parents have for their children, the way a child carries both the being and likeness of their parents in a wonderful way, especially the deep connection mothers feel for those they have given birth to!
15.5: For as much as mothers are naturally gentle and bring many children into the world, they are even more deeply attached to them.
15.6: Of all mothers, the mother of the seven was the most loving, having developed a deep affection for her children through seven births.
15.7: Because of all the pain she endured for each one, she was bound to feel deep sympathy for them;
15.8: yet, out of reverence for Elohim, she set aside the temporary deliverance of her children.
15.9: Not only that, but because of her excellent devotion to the Torah, her motherly love for them grew even stronger.
15.10: For her sons were just, self-controlled, courageous, noble, loving toward their family, and so devoted to their mother that they obeyed her even to death by keeping the Torah.
15.11: Even though there were so many reasons for a mother to be moved by love for her children, none of the tortures could make her abandon her conviction.
15.12: Instead, she encouraged each one individually and all together to accept death for the sake of reverence for 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄.
15.13: O qodesh nature and parental love, and the reward of raising children, and unconquerable motherly affection!
15.14: Even as each of them was tortured and burned, her devotion to 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 kept her from wavering.
15.15: She saw her children’s flesh melting by the fire, their limbs trembling on the ground, and the skin of their heads drooping down to their beards like masks.
15.16: O mother, who suffered more bitter pain now than in childbirth!
15.17: O you, the only woman who has shown perfect qodeshah!
15.18: Your firstborn dying did not turn you aside, nor did the second, suffering in agony, nor the third, as he breathed out his life.
15.19: You did not weep when you saw each of their eyes fixed on their torment, and their nostrils showing signs of death!
15.20: When you saw your children’s flesh piled upon flesh, heads severed upon heads, the dead falling on the dead, and your children turned by torture into a burial ground, you did not mourn.
15.21: Not even the songs of sirens or swans draw listeners as powerfully as the voices of your children calling to you in their suffering!
15.22: What kind of torment did the mother herself endure as her sons were tortured on the wheel and by fire!
15.23: But her reverence for 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 gave her strength in her suffering, allowing her to set aside her motherly love for a time.
15.24: Even as she saw the death of her seven children, this noble mother, after one last embrace, put aside her feelings through her trust in Elohim.
15.25: It was as if, in her own heart, she saw strong counselors—her natural instincts, her motherhood, her love for her children, and the sight of their torture—
15.26: and she held two votes: one for their death, and one for their survival.
15.27: She did not choose to save her children for only a short time.
15.28: But this daughter of Aḇraham remembered his qodesh courage.
15.29: O qodesh mother of a nation, defender of the Torah, protector of reverence for 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄, and leader in the struggle of the heart!
15.30: O you who endured more nobly than men, and showed more courage than any man!
15.31: For just as Noaḥ’s ark carried the world through the flood,
15.32: so you, guardian of the Torah, surrounded by a flood of emotions and battered by the storms of your children’s suffering, stood firm for reverence for 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄.

16.1: If even a woman—an elderly mother of seven sons—endured watching her children’s suffering all the way to death, then it must be admitted that reverent reasoning truly rules over the emotions.
16.2: So I have shown that not only men have mastered their emotions, but also that a woman could despise the greatest torments.
16.3: The lions around Dani’ĕl were not as fierce, nor the furnace for Misha’ĕl burning with such intense fire, as the natural love for her children that burned within her when she saw her seven sons tortured.
16.4: But with reverent reasoning, the mother overcame emotions so strong and powerful.
16.5: We should also consider this: if the woman had been fainthearted as their mother, she would have mourned for them, and perhaps might have said:
16.6: “Oh, how wretched and miserable I am, who after bearing seven sons, am now the mother of none.
16.7: O seven useless childbirths, seven fruitless labors, empty nursing, and sorrowful feedings at the breast.
16.8: In vain, for your sake, my sons, I have endured many pains and the harder worries of raising you.
16.9: Alas, some of you are unmarried, and some married with no benefit; I will not see your children, nor have the joy of being a grandmother.
16.10: Oh, that I, who once had many beautiful children, am now a lonely widow full of sorrow!
16.11: Nor, if I die, will I have a son to bury me.” But with such words, this qodesh and Elohim-fearing mother did not weep for any of them.
16.12: She did not turn any of them away from death, nor mourn for them as if they were dead.
16.13: Instead, with a mind as strong as diamond, and as if she were giving birth again to her full number of sons for immortality, she urged them on to die for reverence.
16.14: O woman, soldier of Elohim for reverence, you—aged and a woman—have conquered even a tyrant through endurance; and though weak, have shown yourself stronger in actions and words.
16.15: For when you were seized with your children, you stood watching Eli’ezer being tortured, and said to your sons in the Iḇri tongue,
16.16: “My sons, you are called to a noble contest as witnesses for the nation. Strive eagerly for the Torah of your people.
16.17: For it would be shameful if this old man endured pain for the sake of righteousness, but you, being younger, were afraid of the tortures.
16.18: Remember that through Elohim you received life and have enjoyed it.
16.19: Therefore, you should endure every suffering because of Elohim.
16.20: For our father Aḇraham was also willing to offer up Yitsḥaq our ancestor, and did not flinch when he saw his own hand holding the sword over him.
16.21: The righteous Dani’ĕl was thrown to the lions; and Ḥananyah, Azaryah, and Misha’ĕl were thrown into a blazing furnace, yet they endured through Elohim.
16.22: So you, having the same trust in Elohim, do not be troubled.
16.23: For it would not make sense for those who know reverence not to stand firm in the face of troubles.
16.24: With these words, the mother of seven encouraged each of her sons, urging and persuading them not to break the command of Elohim.
16.25: They also saw that those who die for Elohim live to Elohim, like Aḇraham, Yitsḥaq, Ya’aqoḇ, and all the patriarchs.

17.1: Some of the spearbearers said that when she was about to be seized to be put to death, she threw herself onto the pyre rather than let them touch her body.
17.2: O mother, who together with your seven children overcame the violence of the tyrant, nullified his wicked plans, and showed the nobility of belief!
17.3: For you, like a house firmly built on the foundation of your children, withstood the blows of torture without wavering.
17.4: So take courage, qodesh-minded mother! Hold fast to the firm hope of your steadfastness with 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄.
17.5: The moon with the stars in the shamayim is not as esteemed as you, who are honored before 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 and set in the sky with your sons, whom you enlightened with belief to shine like the stars.
17.6: For your motherhood was in the manner of a child of Aḇraham.
17.7: If it were Lawful for us to paint your story of belief on a tablet, those who saw it would not shrink back at seeing the mother of seven children enduring all kinds of torture to death for the sake of belief.
17.8: It would have been fitting to inscribe on the tomb itself these words as a memorial for the nation:
17.9: "Here an aged kohĕn, an aged woman, and seven sons are buried, killed by the violence of a tyrant who tried to destroy the community of the Iḇrim.
17.10: They also avenged their nation, looking to Elohim and enduring torments to death."
17.11: For it was truly a contest of the divine that they accomplished.
17.12: At that time, virtue presided over the contest, granting victory through endurance—immortality and eternal life.
17.13: Eli’ezer was the first to enter the contest. The mother of the seven children joined in, and their family contended together.
17.14: The tyrant was their opponent; the world and all living people were the spectators.
17.15: Reverence for Elohim triumphed and crowned its own athletes.
17.16: Who did not admire these champions of true Torah? Who was not amazed?
17.17: Even the tyrant himself and all his council were amazed at their endurance.
17.18: Because of this, they now stand beside the divine throne and live a happy life.
17.19: For Mosheh says, "All the qodesh ones are under Your hands."
17.20: These, having been made qodesh through Elohim, have been honored not only with this esteem, but also because through them, the enemy did not overcome our nation.
17.21: That tyrant was punished, and their land was purified.
17.22: For they became a ransom for the sin of the nation. Divine Providence saved Yisra’ĕl, who had been afflicted, by the blood of these righteous ones and by their death that turned away wrath.
17.23: For the tyrant Antioḵos, seeing their courageous virtue and endurance in torture, held up their endurance as an example to his soldiers.
17.24: They proved to him to be noble and brave in land battles and sieges, and he conquered and captured the towns of all his enemies.

18.1: O children of Yisra’ĕl, descendants of the seed of Aḇraham, obey this Torah and be reverent in every way,
18.2: knowing that reverent reasoning rules over the emotions, not only inwardly but outwardly as well.
18.3: Therefore, those who gave up their bodies to suffering for the sake of reverence were not only admired by people, but were considered worthy of a portion from Elohim.
18.4: Through them, the nation gained peace, and by renewing the observance of the Torah in their land, they drove the enemy out.
18.5: The tyrant Antioḵos was punished both on earth and is punished now after his death; for when he was completely unable to force the sons of Yisra’ĕl to adopt foreign customs and abandon the ways of their fathers,
18.6: he left Yerushalayim and made war against Paras.
18.7: The righteous mother of the seven children also spoke to her offspring, saying: “I was a pure maiden and did not go beyond my father’s house, but I guarded the rib from which woman was made.
18.8: No destroyer of the desert or attacker of the plain harmed me, nor did the deceitful, destructive serpent take away my chaste virginity. I remained with my husband during the time of my maturity.
18.9: When you, my children, reached maturity, your father died. He was happy! For having sought a fruitful life in children, he did not have to mourn the loss of his children.
18.10: While he was with you, he taught you the Torah and the prophets.
18.11: He read to you about the slaying of Heḇel by Qayin, the offering up of Yitsḥaq, and the imprisonment of Yosĕph.
18.12: He told you about the zealous Pineḥas, and informed you about Ḥananyah, Azaryah, and Misha’ĕl in the fire.
18.13: He gave esteem to Dani’ĕl, who was in the lions’ den, and called him happy.
18.14: He reminded you of the writing of Yeshayahu, which says, “Even if you pass through the fire, it will not burn you.”
18.15: He sang to you Dawiḏ, the psalmist, who says, “Many are the afflictions of the righteous.”
18.16: He spoke the proverbs of Shelomoh, who says, “He is a tree of life to all who do His will.”
18.17: He confirmed what Yeḥezqĕl said: “Will these dry bones live?”
18.18: For he did not forget the song that Mosheh taught, declaring, “I kill, and I make alive.”
18.19: This is our life and the length of our days.
18.20: O that bitter, and yet not bitter, day when the cruel tyrant of the Yawanites, quenching fire with fire in his savage cauldrons, brought the seven sons of the daughter of Aḇraham to the rack and to all his tortures!
18.21: He pierced their eyes, cut out their tongues, and put them to death with various tortures.
18.22: Therefore, the retribution of Elohim pursued and will pursue that wicked wretch.
18.23: But the children of Aḇraham, together with their victorious mother, are gathered to the assembly of their father, having received pure and immortal lives from Elohim.
18.24: To Him be esteem forever and ever. Amĕn.

2.1: Is it any wonder? When the desires of the being for what is beautiful are blocked,
2.2: this is why the self-controlled Yosĕph is praised—because by reasoning, he overcame the indulgence of the senses.
2.3: For even though he was young and at the age for sexual relations, he used reasoning to overcome the urges of his emotions.
2.4: It’s not just the urge for sensual pleasure, but every desire, that reasoning can master.
2.5: For example, the Torah says, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, nor anything that belongs to your neighbor.”
2.6: So, since the Torah has forbidden us to desire, I can even more easily convince you that reasoning can rule over our lusts, just as it does the emotions that get in the way of justice.
2.7: For how else can a person who eats alone, a glutton, or a drunkard be corrected, unless it’s clear that reasoning rules over the emotions?
2.8: So, a person who lives by the Torah, even if he loves money, immediately restrains himself by lending to the needy without interest and cancelling the debt in the seventh year.
2.9: If someone is greedy, the Torah, working through reasoning, rules over him so that he doesn’t gather every last bit of his crops or grapes. In other ways too, we see that reasoning conquers his emotions.
2.10: For the Torah even overcomes affection for parents, not giving up virtue for their sake.
2.11: It prevails over love for one’s wife, correcting her if she breaks the Torah.
2.12: It rules over the love parents have for their children, since they punish them for wrongdoing. It even dominates close friendships, correcting friends when they do evil.
2.13: Don’t think it’s strange to say that reasoning, for the sake of the Torah, can even conquer hatred.
2.14: It doesn’t allow you to cut down the fruit trees of an enemy, but protects them from destruction and gathers up what has fallen.
2.15: Reasoning seems to rule over even the strongest emotions, like the desire for power, empty boasting, and slander.
2.16: For a self-controlled mind rejects all these harmful emotions, just as it does anger; for it even masters that.
2.17: For example, Mosheh, when he was angry with Dathan and Aḇiram, did nothing to them in his anger, but controlled his anger with reasoning.
2.18: For a self-controlled mind, as I said, can rise above the emotions, correcting some and getting rid of others.
2.19: Why else did our wise father Ya’aqoḇ rebuke Shim’on and Lĕwi for irrationally killing all the Sheḵemites, saying, “Cursed be their anger!”?
2.20: For if reasoning didn’t have the power to control angry emotions, he wouldn’t have said this.
2.21: For when Elohim created man, He put within him both emotions and a moral nature.
2.22: At that time, He set the mind above all as the qodesh leader, working through the senses.
2.23: He gave this mind a Torah, and by living according to it, the mind will rule in a self-controlled, just, good, and courageous way.
2.24: So someone might ask, if reasoning rules over the emotions, does it have no control over forgetfulness and ignorance?

3.1: This argument is extremely unreasonable, because reasoning doesn’t control its own emotions, but rather those of the body.
3.2: So, even if none of you can completely get rid of desire, reasoning can help you avoid being ruled by it.
3.3: You might not be able to remove anger from your being, but you can resist it.
3.4: You may not be able to wipe out malice, but reasoning can work with you so you don’t give in to it.
3.5: Reasoning doesn’t erase emotions, but stands against them.
3.6: This becomes clearer when we look at the thirst of Meleḵ Dawiḏ.
3.7: After Dawiḏ had been fighting the Pelishtites all day, he and the soldiers of his nation killed many of them.
3.8: When evening came, exhausted and sweating, he returned to the royal tent, where the whole army of our ancestors was camped.
3.10: but the meleḵ, though extremely thirsty and surrounded by many springs, couldn’t satisfy his thirst with them.
3.11: Instead, he felt an irrational craving for water from the enemy’s camp, which grew stronger and overwhelmed him.
3.12: Seeing the meleḵ’s longing, two brave young soldiers, out of respect for his desire, armed themselves and, taking a pitcher, crossed over the enemy’s ramparts.
3.13: They slipped past the gate guards and searched the entire enemy camp.
3.14: They boldly found the spring and filled the pitcher with water for the meleḵ.
3.15: But Dawiḏ, though desperately thirsty, reasoned that drinking water gained at the risk of blood would endanger his being.
3.16: So, putting reasoning above his desire, he poured out the water as an offering to 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄.
3.17: A self-controlled mind can overcome emotional urges and put out the fires of passion,
3.18: and can endure even extreme bodily pain, and through the strength of reasoning, reject all attacks from the emotions.
3.19: Now, let’s look at an example of self-controlled reasoning from history.
3.20: When our ancestors enjoyed peace by following the Torah and prospered, Seleukus Nikanor, meleḵ of Asia, even gave them money for service to 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 and accepted their way of governing.
3.21: But then, some people introduced new practices that disrupted harmony, and as a result, they suffered in many ways.

4.1: There was a man named Shim’on, who opposed an honorable and good man who had once held the office of kohĕn ha’gadol for life, named Onyah. After slandering Onyah in every way, Shim’on couldn’t harm him among the people, so he left as an exile, intending to betray his own country.
4.2: When he came to Apollonios, the military governor of Suria, Phoinikĕ, and Kilikia, he said,
4.3: “Out of loyalty to the meleḵ’s interests, I have come to inform you that tens of thousands in private wealth are stored in the treasuries of Yerushalayim, which do not belong to the Miqdash, but to Meleḵ Seleukus.”
4.4: Apollonios, after learning the details, praised Shim’on for his concern for the meleḵ’s interests, and went up to Seleukus to inform him about the treasure.
4.5: Receiving authority regarding this, he quickly entered our land with the accursed Shim’on and a very large force,
4.6: saying that he came with the meleḵ’s orders to take the private money from the treasury.
4.7: The nation, outraged at this announcement, replied that it was extremely unjust for those who had entrusted deposits to the qodesh treasury to be deprived of them, and resisted as much as they could.
4.8: But Apollonios went away with threats into the Miqdash.
4.9: The kohenim, along with the women and children, pleaded with Elohim to shield the qodesh, despised place.
4.10: As Apollonios was going up with his armed force to seize the treasure, messengers from shamayim appeared riding on horses, shining in armor, filling them all with great fear and trembling.
4.11: Apollonios collapsed, nearly dead, in the court open to all nations, stretched out his hands to shamayim, and begged the Iḇrim, with tears, to pray for him and remove the wrath of the army of the shamayim.
4.12: He admitted that he had sinned and deserved death, and promised that if he were saved, he would proclaim to all people the blessedness of the qodesh place.
4.13: Onyah the kohĕn ha’gadol, moved by these words, and also concerned that Meleḵ Seleukus would not think Apollonios was killed by human means instead of by punishment from above, prayed for him;
4.14: and so, unexpectedly saved, Apollonios left to report to the meleḵ what had happened to him.
4.15: But after the death of Meleḵ Seleukus, his son Antioḵos Epiphanĕs succeeded to the throne—a terrible man filled with arrogant pride.
4.16: He removed Onyah from the office of kohĕn ha’gadol and appointed his brother Yason as kohĕn ha’gadol,
4.17: who had agreed, if given this authority, to pay three thousand six hundred and sixty talents each year.
4.18: He gave him the office of kohĕn ha’gadol and rule over the nation.
4.19: He changed the way of life of the people and corrupted their civil customs into all kinds of lawlessness.
4.20: He not only built a gymnasium on the very citadel of our land, but also neglected the guardianship of the Miqdash.
4.21: Because of this, vengeance from above was provoked and stirred up Antioḵos himself against them.
4.22: While at war with Ptolemaeus in Mitsrayim, he heard that a rumor of his death had spread, and that the people of Yerushalayim had greatly rejoiced, so he quickly marched against them.
4.23: After subduing them, he issued a decree that anyone who lived according to the ancestral laws should be put to death.
4.24: When he could not destroy obedience to the Torah by his decrees, and saw that all his threats and punishments were ineffective,
4.25: even women, because they continued to circumcise their children, were thrown down a precipice along with them, knowing in advance the punishment.
4.26: When his decrees were ignored by the people, he himself forced everyone of this nation, through torture and by making them taste forbidden meats, to renounce the belief of the Yahuḏim.

5.1: The tyrant Antioḵos, therefore, sat in public with his advisors on a high platform, surrounded by his armed soldiers standing in a circle.
5.2: He ordered his guards to seize every one of the Iḇrim and force them to eat swine’s meat and food offered to idols.
5.3: If any refused to eat the forbidden food, they were to be tortured on the wheel and then killed.
5.4: When many had been captured, a leading man from the assembly, an Iḇri named Eli’ezer, a kohĕn by family, a lawyer by profession, advanced in age and well-known to many of the meleḵ’s followers, was brought before him.
5.6: “Old man, before you are tortured, I advise you to taste the swine’s meat and save your life. I respect your age and gray hair, which you have had for so long, but it seems to me you are not wise to keep holding onto the superstition of the Yahuḏim.
5.7: Since nature has given you the excellent meat of this animal, why do you reject it?
5.8: It seems foolish not to enjoy what is pleasant and not shameful, and to refuse the gifts of nature because of ideas about sin.
5.9: You will be acting even more foolishly, I think, if you follow empty ideas about the truth.
5.10: You will also be insulting me, which will only bring punishment on yourself.
5.11: Won’t you give up your pointless philosophy, let go of your foolish ideas, and, with understanding fitting your age, look for a wise and practical path?
5.12: Won’t you listen to my kind advice and have pity on your own years?
5.13: Remember, if there is any power watching over your religion, it will forgive you for any breaking of the Torah you do under force.”
5.14: While the tyrant tried to persuade him to eat the forbidden meat, Eli’ezer asked for permission to speak.
5.15: When he was allowed to speak, he began to address the people:
5.16: “We, Antioḵos, who believe we live under a divine Torah, consider no force as strong as our duty to obey that Torah.
5.17: Therefore, we believe we must not break the Torah in any way.
5.18: Even if our Torah, as you claim, were not truly from Elohim, and if we wrongly thought it was, we still would have no right to destroy our sense of reverence.
5.19: Don’t think eating unclean meat is a small matter.
5.20: For breaking the Torah, whether in small or great things, is equally serious;
5.21: because in either case, the Torah is being disregarded.
5.22: But you mock our way of life, as if we follow it without reason.
5.23: Yet it teaches us self-control, so we rise above all pleasures and desires; and it trains us in courage, so we willingly endure every hardship.
5.24: It teaches us justice, so that in all we do, we give what is right. It teaches us reverence, so we properly worship the one and only Elohim.
5.25: That is why we do not eat what is unclean; because we believe the Torah was given by Elohim, we are sure that the Creator of the world, in giving His commands, understands our nature.
5.26: He has told us to eat what is good for our beings, and forbidden what is not.
5.27: But you, like a tyrant, not only force us to break the Torah, but also to eat, so you can mock us as we eat what is forbidden.
5.28: But you will not have this reason to laugh at me,
5.29: nor will I break the qodesh promises of my ancestors to keep the Torah.
5.30: No, not even if you tear out my eyes or destroy my insides.
5.31: I am not so old or lacking in courage that I cannot be strong in mind and defend my faith.
5.32: So go ahead, prepare your wheels and light a hotter fire.
5.33: I will not pity my old age so much as to break the Torah of my people for my own sake.
5.34: I will not betray you, O Torah, my teacher, or abandon you, O beloved self-control!
5.35: I will not shame you, O Reason, or deny you, O honored kehunnah and knowledge of the Torah.
5.36: Mouth! You will not defile my old age or the full measure of a faithful life.
5.37: My ancestors will welcome me as pure, not having feared your force, even to death.
5.38: For you may rule like a tyrant over the wicked, but you will not rule over my thoughts about reverence, either by your words or your actions.”

6.1: When Eli’ezer had answered the tyrant's appeals in this way, the spearbearers came up and roughly dragged Eli’ezer to the instruments of torture.
6.2: First, they stripped the old man, who was adorned with the beauty of reverence.
6.3: Then, tying back his arms and hands, they contemptuously flogged him.
6.4: A herald standing opposite shouted, “Obey the commands of the meleḵ!”
6.5: But the courageous and truly noble Eli’ezer, as if being tortured in a dream, paid no attention.
6.6: Lifting his eyes upward to the shamayim, the old man's flesh was torn off by the scourges, his blood streamed down, and his sides were pierced through.
6.7: Collapsing to the ground because his body could not endure the pain, he still kept his reasoning upright and unyielding.
6.8: Then one of the harsh spearbearers rushed at him and began to kick him in the side to force him to get up after he had fallen.
6.9: But he endured the pain, despised the cruelty, and persevered through the humiliation.
6.10: Like a noble athlete, the old man, when struck, overcame his torturers.
6.11: His face sweating and gasping for breath, he was admired even by his torturers for his courage.
6.12: Therefore, partly out of pity for his old age,
6.13: partly from sympathy as acquaintances, and partly in admiration of his endurance, some of the meleḵ’s attendants said,
6.14: “Why do you destroy yourself needlessly, O Eli’ezer, with these sufferings?
6.15: We will bring you some meat cooked by yourself, and you can save yourself by pretending you have eaten swine’s flesh.”
6.16: Eli’ezer, as if this advice tortured him even more, cried out,
6.17: “Let us, who are children of Aḇraham, not be so badly advised as to give in and use a shameful deception.
6.18: For it would be unreasonable, if after living all our years in truth and carefully guarding our character, we would now turn back
6.19: and become an example of irreverence to the young, showing them how to eat what is defiled.
6.20: It would be disgraceful if we lived on for just a short time, only to be despised by everyone for cowardice,
6.21: and to be condemned by the tyrant for not standing firm to the death for our Torah.
6.22: Therefore you, O children of Aḇraham, die nobly for your belief.
6.23: You spearbearers of the tyrant, why do you delay?”
6.24: Seeing him so steadfast in the face of suffering, and unmoved by their pity, they led him to the fire.
6.25: Then, using their wickedly designed instruments, they burned him in the fire and poured foul-smelling liquids into his nostrils.
6.26: When he was finally burned down to the bone and about to die, he lifted his eyes toward Elohim and said,
6.27: “You know, O Elohim, that when I could have been saved, I am killed for the sake of the Torah by tortures of fire.
6.28: Be merciful to Your people, and let my punishment be enough for them.
6.29: Let my blood be a cleansing for them, and take my life in exchange for theirs.”
6.30: After saying this, the qodesh man died, noble in his suffering, and even in the agony of death he resisted with his reasoning for the sake of the Torah.
6.31: It is clear, then, that reverent reasoning rules over the emotions.
6.32: For if the emotions had been stronger than reasoning, I would have shown you proof of their mastery.
6.33: But now, since reasoning has conquered the emotions, we rightly give it the highest place.
6.34: It is only right that we recognize that the power belongs to reasoning, since it overcomes external suffering.
6.35: It would be absurd if this were not so. I have shown that reasoning not only masters pain, but is also superior to pleasures, and can withstand them.

7.1: The reasoning of our father Eli’ezer was like a skilled pilot, steering the ship of reverence through the sea of emotions,
7.2: and though mocked by the threats of the tyrant and battered by the waves of torture,
7.3: he never turned the rudder of reverence aside until he reached the harbor of victory over death.
7.4: No besieged city has ever resisted so many and varied war machines as that qodesh man did, when his reverent being was tested by the fiery ordeal of tortures and rackings, and he moved his attackers through the religious reasoning that protected him.
7.5: For father Eli’ezer, showing his character, broke the raging waves of emotion like a solid cliff.
7.6: O kohĕn worthy of the kehunnah! You did not defile your qodesh teeth, nor let your appetite—which always embraced what is clean and Lawful—become a partner in profaneness.
7.7: O one in harmony with the Torah, and wise man devoted to a life with Elohim!
7.8: Those who serve the Torah, even at the risk of their own blood, and defend it with generous sweat, even to death, should have such character.
7.9: You, father, have established our right order with your endurance; and by valuing our past service, you prevented its destruction, and through your actions, you have proven the truth of wisdom.
7.10: O elder more powerful than tortures, aged one stronger than fire, greatest ruler over the emotions, Eli’ezer!
7.11: For just as father Aharon, armed with a censer, rushed through the consuming fire and overcame the flame-bearing messenger,
7.12: so Eli’ezer, a descendant of Aharon, though wasting away by fire, did not give up his reasoning.
7.13: What is most amazing is that, though he was an old man, his body worn out, his muscles relaxed, and his sinews tired, he regained his strength.
7.14: By the spirit of reasoning, and the reasoning of Yitsḥaq, he overcame the many-headed torture rack.
7.15: O happy old age, and honored gray hair, and life obedient to the Torah, which the faithful seal of death perfected.
7.16: If an old man, through reverence, could despise tortures even to death, then certainly reverent reasoning rules over the emotions.
7.17: But some might say, “Not everyone conquers emotions, since not all have wise reasoning.”
7.18: But only those who have devoted themselves to reverence with all their heart can truly master the emotions of the flesh:
7.19: those who believe that to Elohim they do not die; for, like our fathers, Aḇraham, Yitsḥaq, and Ya’aqoḇ, they live to Elohim.
7.20: So it is no argument that some people with weak reasoning are ruled by their emotions,
7.21: since what person, living reverently by the full rule of wisdom and believing in Elohim,
7.22: and knowing that it is a happy thing to endure all kinds of hardship for virtue, would not, for the sake of reverence, master his emotions?
7.23: For only the wise and brave person is master over his emotions.
7.24: That is why even boys, trained in the wisdom of reverent reasoning, have overcome even harsher tortures;
7.25: for when the tyrant was clearly defeated in his first attempt, being unable to force the old man to eat the unclean thing,

8.1: Then, deeply moved with emotion, he ordered that other adult Iḇrim be brought in, and said that if they would eat the unclean food, they should be released after eating; but if they refused, they were to be tortured even more severely.
8.2: After the tyrant gave this command, seven brothers were brought before him, along with their elderly mother. They were handsome, modest, well-born, and altogether attractive.
8.3: When the tyrant saw them surrounding their mother like a dance, he was pleased with them. Impressed by their dignified and innocent behavior, he smiled at them, called them closer, and said,
8.4: “Young men, I look on each of you with favor and admire your beauty. Honoring such a large family, I not only advise you not to follow the madness of the old man who was tortured before you,
8.5: but I urge you to give in and enjoy my friendship. I have the power not only to punish those who disobey my commands, but also to reward those who obey.
8.6: Trust me, and you will receive positions of authority in my government, if you abandon your national way of life,
8.7: and, by adopting the Yawanite way of life, change your customs and enjoy the pleasures of youth.
8.8: But if you provoke me by your disobedience, you will force me to destroy every one of you with terrible tortures.
8.9: Have mercy on yourselves, for even though I am your enemy, I feel compassion for your youth and good looks.
8.10: Don’t you realize that if you disobey, the only thing left for you is to die in torment?”
8.11: After saying this, he ordered the instruments of torture to be brought out, hoping that fear would persuade them to eat the unclean meat.
8.12: When the spearman brought out the wheels, racks, hooks, cauldrons, pans, finger-racks, iron hands and wedges, and bellows, the tyrant continued:
8.13: “Be afraid, young men, and the righteousness you worship will forgive you if you break it under compulsion.”
8.14: But after hearing these persuasive words and seeing the terrifying instruments, they were not afraid at all. Instead, they answered the tyrant’s arguments and, through their wise reasoning, overcame his power.
8.15: Let’s think about this: If any of them had been weak or cowardly, what arguments would they have used except these?
8.16: “How miserable and foolish we are! When the meleḵ urges us and offers us his generosity, shouldn’t we obey him?
8.17: Why do we encourage ourselves with empty advice and risk disobedience that leads to death?
8.18: Shouldn’t we, brothers, fear the instruments of torture, consider the threats of torment, and avoid this empty pride and destructive arrogance?
8.19: Let’s have pity on our youth and feel for the years of our mother.
8.20: Let’s remember that we will die as rebels.
8.21: 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄’s justice will forgive us if we fear the meleḵ out of necessity.
8.22: Why give up such a sweet life and deprive ourselves of this pleasant world?
8.23: Let’s not resist necessity or seek empty honor by bringing torture on ourselves.
8.24: Even the Torah itself wouldn’t put us to death just because we fear torture.
8.25: Why has such fierce zeal taken hold of us, and why do we cling to such deadly stubbornness, when we could live peacefully under the meleḵ?”
8.26: But the young men did not say or even think anything like this when they were about to be tortured.
8.27: They fully understood the suffering ahead and were ready to endure the pain.
8.28: So as soon as the tyrant stopped urging them to eat the unclean food, they all spoke with one voice, as if from the same heart, and said:

9.1: “Why do you hesitate, tyrant? We are more willing to die than to break the commands of our fathers.
9.2: We would bring shame on our fathers if we didn’t obey the Torah and let knowledge guide us.
9.3: Tyrant, you who advise breaking the Torah, don’t pity us more than we pity ourselves, even though you hate us.
9.4: We see your escape as worse than death.
9.5: You try to frighten us with threats of torture and death, as if you learned nothing from the death of Eli’ezer.
9.6: But if aged men of the Iḇrim have died for the sake of reverence after enduring torture, then even more should we, the younger, die—despising your cruel tortures, which our elderly teacher overcame.
9.7: Go ahead and try, tyrant. If you kill us for our reverence, don’t think you harm us by torturing us.
9.8: Because through this suffering and endurance, we will receive the rewards of uprightness.
9.9: But you, for your wicked and tyrannical slaughter of us, will suffer everlasting torment by fire from 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄’s vengeance.”
9.10: When they said this, the tyrant was not only furious with them for disobeying, but also enraged at their lack of gratitude.
9.11: So, at his command, the torturers brought the oldest of them, tore his tunic, and bound his hands and arms on each side with straps.
9.12: After they had beaten him hard with no result, they threw him onto the wheel.
9.13: The noble young man, stretched out on it, became dislocated.
9.14: With every limb out of joint, he condemned the tyrant, saying,
9.15: “Most cursed tyrant, enemy of shamayim’s justice, and cruel-hearted, I am not a murderer or a blasphemer whom you torture, but a defender of the Torah of Elohim.”
9.16: When the guards said, “Agree to eat, and you’ll be freed from your torture,”
9.17: he replied, “Your wheel, cursed lackeys, is not powerful enough to silence my reasoning. Cut off my limbs, burn my flesh, twist my joints.
9.18: Through all my suffering, I will show you that the children of the Iḇrim alone are unconquered for the sake of uprightness.”
9.19: While he was saying this, they piled up fuel, set it on fire, and stretched him even more on the wheel.
9.20: The wheel was covered in blood. The hot ashes were soaked by the dripping gore, and pieces of flesh were scattered around the axles of the device.
9.21: Even though his bones were now shattered, the courageous and Aḇrahamic youth did not groan.
9.22: But as if transformed by fire into immortality, he bravely endured the torture, saying,
9.23: “Follow my example, brothers. Never abandon your post or give up our brotherhood in courage. Fight the qodesh and honorable fight for reverence,
9.24: so that our just and fatherly Providence, showing mercy to the nation, will punish this wicked tyrant.”
9.25: After saying this, the respected young man suddenly died.
9.26: As everyone admired his brave spirit, the guards brought forward the second oldest, put iron gloves with sharp hooks on him, and bound him to the rack.
9.27: When they asked if he would eat before being tortured, they heard his noble answer.
9.28: After they had violently torn all the flesh from his neck to his chin with the iron gloves, the savage men ripped the very skin from his head, but he endured this suffering with strength and said,
9.29: “How sweet is every kind of death for the reverence of our fathers!” Then he said to the tyrant,
9.30: “Don’t you see, most cruel of all tyrants, that you are now suffering more than I am, as your arrogant idea of tyranny is defeated by our perseverance for our reverence?
9.31: I ease my pain with the joy that comes from uprightness.
9.32: But you are tormented by threats because of your wickedness. You will not escape, most corrupt tyrant, the vengeance of 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄’s wrath.”
